# Book of Giants — Reader's Guide
*HESED Reader's Guide | Dead Sea Scrolls Sectarian Texts*

---

## At a Glance

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Manuscripts | 4Q203, 4Q530, 4Q531, 4Q532, 1Q23, 1Q24, 2Q26, 6Q8 (fragments from multiple caves) |
| Language | Aramaic |
| Script | Jewish square script |
| Date of Composition | c. 2nd–1st century BCE |
| Genre | Apocalyptic narrative — expansion of 1 Enoch 6–16 |
| Extent | 12 reconstructed sections; all heavily fragmentary |
| Key Characters | Ohya, Hahya (the giant brothers), Mahaway, Enoch, the Watchers |
| Canonical Parallel | Genesis 6:1–4 (the Nephilim); 1 Enoch 6–16 (the Watchers) |
| Remarkable Survival | Adopted by Manichaeism (3rd c. CE); fragments found as far as China in Sogdian, Middle Persian, and Uighur |
| Discovery | Cave 1 (1947), Cave 4 (1952), Cave 6 (1952) |

---

## Sections Overview

**Section 1 — The Giants on Earth**
Fragmentary introductory material establishing the situation: the Watchers have descended, taken wives, and their offspring — the Giants — now fill the earth with violence and bloodshed.

**Section 2 — The Giants' Dreams (Ohya and Hahya)**
The two giant brothers Ohya and Hahya experience disturbing dreams. The content involves destruction — a garden, trees being felled, only roots surviving. The dreams are clearly prophetic but the Giants do not understand them. This section is the theological and dramatic heart of the text.

**Section 3 — The Assembly of the Giants**
The Giants gather to discuss their dreams. They are frightened. They know something terrible is coming but cannot interpret the signs.

**Section 4 — Mahaway Sent to Enoch**
The Giants decide to send a messenger to Enoch, the one human who lives at the edge of the world and has access to divine knowledge. Mahaway — another giant figure — is commissioned as the messenger. His journey involves a remarkable scene in which he flies toward Enoch, passing over the waters.

**Section 5 — Enoch Reads the Heavenly Tablets**
Enoch receives the Giants' appeal and reads from the heavenly tablets — the cosmic record of divine judgment. His verdict is unambiguous: there is no forgiveness, no escape. The Watchers and their offspring are condemned. The flood is coming.

**Section 6 — Enoch's Second Letter**
Enoch sends a written response back to the Giants via Mahaway. This detail — a written letter from Enoch — is significant: it treats the heavenly revelation as something that can be inscribed and transmitted. The letter confirms the judgment.

**Section 7 — The Garden/Tree Dream Interpreted**
The dream of the garden with three roots surviving is decoded: the three surviving roots represent Noah and his sons. All else — the Giants included — will be destroyed.

**Sections 8–12 — Fragments of Violence and End**
The remaining reconstructed sections are extremely fragmentary. They appear to depict the increasingly violent behavior of the Giants in the days before the flood, confrontations among the Giants themselves, and the approach of judgment.

---

## The World Behind the Text

Genesis 6:1–4 is one of the most compressed and mysterious passages in the entire Torah:

> "When human beings began to multiply on the face of the ground... the sons of God saw that the daughters of humans were beautiful, and they took as wives any they chose... The Nephilim were on the earth in those days, and also afterward, when the sons of God went in to the daughters of humans and they bore children to them. These were the mighty ones of old, the men of renown."

This passage provides almost no information about who the "sons of God" are, what the Nephilim are, why this causes the flood, or what the "mighty ones of old" did. By the 3rd–2nd centuries BCE, a massive body of tradition had grown up to fill these gaps, centered in what we now call 1 Enoch.

**The Watchers mythology.** In 1 Enoch 6–16 (the "Book of Watchers"), the "sons of God" become Watchers — a specific rank of heavenly being assigned to observe and guard creation. Two hundred of them descend on Mount Hermon, led by Shemihaza and Azazel, take human wives, and father the Giants (Nephilim). The Giants eat all the food on earth, then begin eating humans, then each other. The Watchers also teach forbidden knowledge: metallurgy, weapons-making, sorcery, cosmetics. The earth cries out. God sends the four archangels to bind the Watchers and destroy the Giants. Enoch serves as the messenger and scribe of heavenly judgment.

**The Book of Giants picks up inside this story.** It is not a retelling of 1 Enoch — it assumes the reader already knows the Watchers narrative and focuses on a subplot that 1 Enoch barely mentions: what happened to the Giants themselves? What did they think was coming? The Book of Giants gives the Giants interiority — dreams, fears, deliberations, a desperate attempt to seek mercy from the one human who has access to God.

**Dreams as divine communication.** In the ancient world, dreams were not psychological events but divine communications. The Giants' inability to interpret their own dreams is theologically significant: they are powerful but not wise. They need Enoch — the human mediator — to decode what the divine realm is saying to them. This is a remarkable inversion: the superhuman beings who corrupted the earth must appeal to a human being for access to divine truth.

---

## Why This Text Was Written

The Book of Giants does not explain the origin of evil — that is what 1 Enoch's Book of Watchers does. The Book of Giants explores what evil looks like from the inside, on its way to judgment.

The Giants are not simply monsters. They are frightened. They have dreams they cannot understand. They send a messenger — they seek to communicate, to plead, possibly to repent. And the answer they receive is: it is too late.

This is a theodicy story — a justification of divine judgment. The flood destroys enormous, seemingly unstoppable beings who have corrupted the earth. The question the text addresses implicitly is: did they know? Did they have the chance to receive warning? The answer the Book of Giants gives is yes — and no mercy was available, because the corruption was too total.

The Qumran community read this text in the context of their own theology of cosmic dualism and eschatological judgment. For them, the story of the Giants was not ancient history but a template: there are powers of darkness at work in the world, they have been condemned, their time is running out, and those who align with them share their fate. The giants' fate prefigured the fate of the wicked at the final judgment.

---

## How to Read This Text

The Book of Giants must be read in fragments — literally. No continuous narrative survives. What scholars have reconstructed is a collage assembled from small overlapping pieces across multiple manuscripts and even multiple languages (the Manichaean versions provide additional material, though they have been modified for their new religious context).

Read 1 Enoch 6–16 first. The Book of Giants makes little sense without knowing the Watchers story. The Giants are already on stage when our text begins; the audience knows why they are condemned; what the Book of Giants adds is the scene of their response.

Notice the reversal: the Giants — who represent superhuman power run amok — are helpless before divine judgment. The only figure who has genuine knowledge and access to God is Enoch, the human being who "walked with God." Power and wisdom are separated. The most powerful beings on earth must beg for information from a human.

Accept the fragmentary nature of the text as part of the reading experience. The gaps are real. The reconstructions are scholarly best-guesses. Where certainty ends, hold conclusions lightly.

---

## The Threads

**The messenger as mediator.** Mahaway's mission to Enoch recasts the mediation theme that runs through the whole Watchers tradition. Enoch is already the mediator who carries the Giants' petition to God in 1 Enoch 13–14. Here, Mahaway is the mediator who carries the Giants' appeal to Enoch. A chain of mediation — Giants to Mahaway, Mahaway to Enoch, Enoch to God — reflects the layered cosmology of Second Temple Judaism: direct access to God is unavailable; communication requires passing through proper channels.

**Dreams and their interpretation.** The garden/tree dream echoes the dream-interpretation cycles in Genesis (Joseph), Daniel (Nebuchadnezzar), and the broader ancient Near Eastern tradition of royal dreams requiring court interpretation. The Giants, like Nebuchadnezzar, have disturbing dreams that foretell their doom, and they need an interpreter outside their own circle. The detail that the surviving roots represent Noah and his sons anticipates the meaning of the flood: not destruction for its own sake, but the preservation of a remnant.

**Written revelation.** Enoch sends a letter. This is not a trivial detail. The practice of writing down divine revelation — treating it as something that can be inscribed, copied, transmitted — is both a claim about the nature of divine communication and a legitimation of the text itself. The Book of Giants is, in some sense, claiming to be a record of the kind of thing Enoch wrote.

**The fate of the Giants as demonic.** Later tradition (1 Enoch 15–16, and echoed in other Second Temple texts) holds that when the Giants were destroyed in the flood, their spirits did not go to Sheol but became wandering demons — the source of evil spirits that afflict the world. The Book of Giants, while fragmentary on this point, participates in this tradition. The Giants are not simply killed; their destruction is the origin of an ongoing demonic presence in the world.

**The global survival of this story.** The Book of Giants traveled further than almost any other Second Temple Jewish text. When Mani (3rd century CE) founded Manichaeism, he incorporated the Book of Giants into his scriptural canon — modifying it to fit his own dualistic cosmology (Enoch became a figure more like Mani himself). Manichaean missionaries carried it east, and fragments in Sogdian, Middle Persian, and Uighur (Turkic) were found at Turfan in Central Asia, along the Silk Road. A Jewish apocalyptic text from Qumran ended up in medieval Chinese-sphere manuscript traditions. The story of the Giants, it turns out, has a remarkable afterlife.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

**This is not Genesis 6:1–4 — it is a story set inside a much larger mythological world.** A reader who comes to the Book of Giants expecting to find it closely tied to the biblical text will be disoriented. The text assumes the entire 1 Enoch Watchers mythology as its backstory. The biblical passage (Gen 6:1–4) is the seed; 1 Enoch is the tree; the Book of Giants is one of the tree's branches.

**The Giants are not simple villains.** The text gives Ohya and Hahya genuine fear and, implicitly, a desire to know their fate and possibly to appeal it. This does not make them sympathetic heroes, but it makes them tragic figures — beings whose corruption was catastrophic but who possessed enough awareness to recognize that judgment was coming. The Book of Giants is not interested in simple moral categories.

**The Manichaean versions are related but not identical.** Scholars use the Manichaean Book of Giants fragments to help reconstruct the Qumran version, but this requires care. Mani adapted the text for his own purposes. In the Manichaean version, the figure corresponding to Enoch carries stronger resonances with Mani's own self-understanding as a revealer. The core narrative is similar, but the theology has been adjusted.

**Mahaway's flight to Enoch is one of the most vivid scenes in DSS literature.** A fragment describes Mahaway flying over the waters like a bird to reach Enoch at the ends of the earth. Even in its fragmentary form, this image is striking. It places the Book of Giants in a tradition of heavenly journeys and cosmic geography — the same tradition that underlies 1 Enoch's throne-room visions and later merkavah mysticism.

**The text was not a curiosity at Qumran — it was read seriously.** Multiple manuscripts of the Book of Giants were found across multiple caves. It was not a marginal text. The Qumran community read it as genuine revelation about the cosmic history of evil, judgment, and the flood. It shaped their worldview.

**The "three roots" dream is a story about survival.** The garden dream — in which all trees are cut down except three roots — is not primarily about destruction. It is about what survives: Noah and his sons, the preserved remnant of humanity through whom creation continues. For the Qumran community, who understood themselves as the faithful remnant of Israel in a corrupt age, this image was not merely historical. It was a mirror.

---

## Why This Text Isn't in Your Bible

The Book of Giants was never part of any biblical canon. It is an expansion of 1 Enoch, which itself sits outside the biblical canon (except in the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition, where 1 Enoch is canonical scripture). Neither the Hebrew Bible nor the New Testament contains the Watchers mythology in the elaborate form these texts assume.

Early Jewish canon formation, crystallizing in the rabbinic period after 70 CE, did not include 1 Enoch or its expansions. The rabbis generally resisted texts that gave too much theological weight to angels, demons, and the corruption of the heavenly order — these traditions were seen as potentially destabilizing to the core monotheistic framework and to human moral responsibility.

Early Christian canon formation worked with the Septuagint and apostolic writings. While a trace of the Watchers tradition appears in the New Testament (2 Peter 2:4, Jude 1:6 mention angels who sinned and are held in chains), these brief references did not bring the full 1 Enoch corpus or the Book of Giants into canonical consideration.

The text's survival is owed to two communities: the Qumran sect, which buried it in caves, and the Manichaeans, who carried a version of it across Central Asia. Neither community's canon overlaps with the biblical canon as historically received.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| c. 300–200 BCE | Book of Watchers (1 Enoch 6–16) composed |
| c. 200–150 BCE | Book of Giants composed in Aramaic, building on 1 Enoch |
| c. 150 BCE – 68 CE | Text copied and held at Qumran in multiple manuscripts |
| c. 68 CE | Qumran community ends; scrolls hidden |
| c. 216 CE | Mani born in Babylonia; begins composing his scriptures |
| c. 240–270 CE | Mani incorporates Book of Giants into Manichaean canon |
| 3rd–7th centuries CE | Manichaean missionaries carry the text east along the Silk Road |
| c. 7th–10th centuries CE | Manichaean Book of Giants fragments copied in Sogdian, Middle Persian, Uighur in Central Asia |
| 1902–1914 CE | German Turfan expeditions discover Manichaean fragments at Turfan (Xinjiang) |
| 1947 CE | Cave 1 discovered; 1Q23–24 among the finds |
| 1952 CE | Cave 4 and Cave 6 discovered; 4Q203, 4Q530–532, 6Q8 recovered |
| 1970s–1990s | Józef Milik publishes and reconstructs the Book of Giants, connecting the DSS fragments to the Manichaean versions |

---

*HESED notes: The Book of Giants is the story that 1 Enoch didn't finish — the inner life of the catastrophe. It takes seriously a question that the biblical flood narrative skips past: the powerful beings who corrupted the world, did they see it coming? Did they try to stop it? The answer is both yes and no: they had dreams, they sent a messenger, they received Enoch's verdict — and there was nothing left to do. For the Qumran community, this was not mythology about the distant past; it was a map of their present, in which the forces of darkness were already condemned and the remnant needed only to hold on. That this story ended up in a Uighur manuscript on the Silk Road, carried by Manichaean monks who thought it illuminated the nature of evil — that is its own kind of testament to the power of the question it asks.*
